Corrupt Kidnappings

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We expose corruption at the highest levels within the SAPS, as leaked audio recordings implicate the head of a kidnapping taskforce in extorting his already traumatised victims.

Unique Selling Point:
We have access to audio recordings of the head of the Crime Intelligence Hostage Rescue team, or HICR, where he is asking for a R40 000 bribe from a family, to solve the case in which their father, a wealthy businessman, was kidnapped. No one else has what we have, and no other media are onto it yet. We would break the story.

Summary:
On the 10th of March this year, Amrath Natha was kidnapped for ransom from his business premises in Johannesburg. Amrath had become the latest victim in an ever increasing crime wave that's hit South Africa's Indian communities, where businessmen are often targeted, kidnapped, and huge ransom's demanded from the distraught families for their release. In Natha's case, the kidnappers were demanding R5 million from the family. The family employed a private security company, and contacted the SAPS for help. The security company, Watchdogz, employed a private investigator named Reshaad Ismail, who was well known for dealing with kidnappings, and who had a good relationship with the head of the kidnapping task team, Col "Touch" Moreme. But as Ismail kept upping the amount he wanted for the work, Watchdogz terminated his employment. Soon thereafter, the family spokesperson, Hiren Rama was called by Col Moreme, and asked to be paid an amount to solve the case. Rama told Watchdogz security about the call, and they contacted the Hawks Anti Corruption unit. Rama started recording the phone - calls between himself and Moreme. In two seperate audio recordings, Moreme can be heard negotiating a price of R40 000. At one point he lowers it to R20 000, but later asks for R40 000 again. We also have further conversations where the money and delivery of the money is discussed.

Further information:
The Hawks tried to catch Moreme receiving the money in a sting operation, but before that could be finalised Amrath Natha was found safe.

The Hawks have obtained the audio recordings and witness statements about the incident, and according to our information Col Moreme has been served with a J175 summons to appear in court relating to charges for the above mentioned on the 12th November 2021.

The Natha family are absolutely terrified of speaking, or even being mentioned in the insert. Amrath Natha is still undergoing trauma counseling, and they are immigrating to another country within the next few days.


The family spokesperson has agreed to be interviewed if we hide his identity.

The family have requested we not mention their names at all - this is a setback but also quite understandable considering the circumstances. We can tell the story using pseudonyms and recreations, as well as the audio recordings.

It seems strange that the prosecutor did not issue an arrest warrant, but rather just the summons. We should ask the NPA why that is.

We will have to give both Ismail and Moreme right's of reply.

Watchdogz Security owner Fuad Vally willing to tell what he knows of the story.

Script:


Corrupt Kidnappings
09 November 2021
First Draft Script


Voice
It’s a scene that would send shivers down anyone’s spine. In this CCTV footage, widely shared on social media in October, a businessman is kidnapped at gunpoint on the streets of Johannesburg. The whole thing is over in a matter of seconds as the heavily armed men shove him into a waiting car. It’s a growing crime trend in South Africa. But here’s an even more disturbing thought - it’s not just the kidnappers you need to be worried about.

Sound Up Leaked Audio
Col Moremi: No that’s why I said to you, lets come to four zero.

Source: Four zero?

Col Moremi: Ja.

Source: Ok, for forty. You’re looking at R40 000 you say?

Col Moremi: Mmm

Link Derek
Kidnappings for ransom are already big business in South Africa, and they’re on the rise. But the recording you’ve just heard is not a negotiation with a kidnapper - it’s a senior police officer allegedly demanding a bribe for the return of the victim.

Voice
This story starts in April this year, with a kidnapping that took place in the Johannesburg CBD. The victim and his family live in fear for their lives, so we’ll call him Mr Adam. Mr Adam was kidnapped from his business by armed men and held hostage for weeks, with the kidnappers demanding millions of rands for his release. At the time, the family asked a close personal friend to act as their representative and liaise with the police and private security companies investigating the case. He’s agreed to speak to us on condition of anonymity. We’ll call him Jake.

Sound Up “Jake”
Jake: There was four guys that came in, and they came in a white taxi. And they picked him up from the shop, he was standing outside. And these guys just put something over his head, picked him up and into the taxi and they drove off.

Derek: Gone…

Jake: Gone.

Voice
The kidnappers used threats of violence to extort their R6 million ransom demand from the terrified family.

Sound Up “Jake”
Derek: Jake, who was speaking to the kidnappers at this time?

Jake: So it was the son who was speaking to the kidnappers and stuff. Basically they said no, we’ll kill your father, we’ll throw him into a truck, a dustbin truck, and we’ll chop him up and… there was a lot of things to that. And I was just getting more scared and more scared…

Voice
Behind the scenes, the police had assembled a kidnapping task team to investigate the case. One of the senior members of the team was Lt Col Thatia “Touch” Moremi from Crime Intelligence.

Sound Up Jake
So he was personally giving me the updates, phoning me at two o clock in the morning, or twelve o clock, ten o clock at night, and giving me updates.

Link Derek
Then the investigation took an unbelievable turn, the victim could be returned at a price, but that money wasn’t going to the kidnappers.

Voice
Jake says Lt Col Moremi allegedly asked him for a bribe to ensure the investigation had a successful outcome. And he says he has the evidence to prove it - he started recording their conversations.

Sound Up Leaked Audio
Jake: So give me a figure, and lets do it, let finish up, I don’t want to waste time.

Col Moremi: If we go for four zero, what do you say? So that I can push these other people.

Jake: Four zero what do you mean? Forty or four thousand?

Col Moremi: Ja, no because I want to push this thing. Wena, that’s why I’m saying tell me so that I can push these people.

Jake: No you tell me, I give you whatever you want. You tell me.

Col Moremi: Mmm

Jake: You tell me.

Col Moremi: Ja let’s not too much, lets go for twenty then.

Jake: Twenty thousand?

Col Moremi: Ja

Jake: Twenty? Ok.

Col Moremi: Ja.

Sound Up Jake
Derek: Jake this is a policeman, asking for a bribe…

Jake: Ja

Derek: to find an elderly man who’d been kidnapped?

Jake: Kidnapped, ja.

Derek: Is that what you’re telling me?

Jake: Jip.


Voice
That’s especially concerning in a country where sophisticated organised crime syndicates are behind many kidnappings. Lizette Lancaster is the Crime Hub Manager for Justice and Violence Prevention at the Institute for Security Studies. She says our kidnapping statistics for the period March 2019 to April 2020 paint a bleak picture.

Sound Up Lizette
For that period alone, we had 6632 kidnappings reported to the police, that translates to an average of about 18 a day.

Voice
One disturbing example is the kidnapping of the Moti siblings, four bothers between the ages of 6 and 15 who were recently abducted and held hostage for weeks before their safe return. Lancaster says the data shows it’s a crime trend that’s on the rise.

Sound Up Lizette
We see that between March 2011 and March 2020, there was a 133% increase in the number of kidnappings reported to the police.

Voice
Jake says after dropping his price to R20 000, Lt Col Moremi, hiked it back up to the initial asking price of R40 000 in a subsequent meeting.

Sound Up Leaked Audio
Col Moremi: No, that’s why I said to you, let’s come to four zero.

Jake: Four zero?

Col Moremi: Ja.

Jake: Ok, so forty, you’re looking at R40 000 you say?

Col Moremi: Mmm

Jake: Alright, no problem, let’s do it, let’s work together, let’s get the old man, and then we can sort out things from there.

Sound Up Jake
Jake: He came back to me and said you know what give me R40 000 now. And we will do the work and whatever it is, and rescue the uncle.

Link Derek
Kidnappings are not always carried out purely to demand a ransom. According to the experts there are as many motives behind these crimes as there are kidnappings on our streets.

Sound Up Herman Bosman
It can be for revenge, it can be for restitution, it can be criminal vendetta type of kidnappings between gangs and groups, it can be purely for money, and also for the sex trade and human trafficking.


Voice
Former police officer Herman Bosman spent over two decades in the service, much of it as the head of the Western Cape’s Hostage Negotiation team.

Sound Up Herman
Derek: 22 years as a hostage negotiator, there must have been so many traumatic and emotional experiences, or is it all just very cool, calm and collected?

Herman: I mean if I think over the decades of doing hostage negotiations, kidnapping incident management, it is absolutely traumatic. I think it is one of the most traumatic experiences that can happen to any family, friends, company. The pain, the heartsore, it’s very far from what movies try and portray. It is very very painful, and it is definitely very inhumane.

Voice
And unfortunately, this isn’t the first time he’s heard of police themselves being involved in extorting money from victims.

Sound Up Herman
Derek: I mean we’re hearing of cases of the police extorting the victims, or the families of the victims, for money to have the cases solved?

Herman: I’ve heard about it as well, ja I think those need to be reported to the correct structures for investigation, and it’s absolutely sick to “profitise" and try and make money out of something as terrible as a kidnapping.

Voice
Jake did take his information to the Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation, the Hawks, who started their own enquiry behind the scenes.

Mr Adam was held hostage for more than two weeks. But even on the day he was finally rescued, Jake says he was still being asked for the R40 000.

Sound Up Leaked Audio
Jake: Hello?

Moremi: Hello? I’m saying our agreement still stands hey?

Jake: Which one is that?

Moremi: How…

Jake: Sorry man, I’m half asleep, that’s why.

Moremi: No that one we spoke about man…

Jake: Oh, ok can I call you in the morning? Can I call you in the morning when I’m awake?

Moremi: Ja.

Jake: Ok

Moremi: That one we said we’ll do it man. You remember you’ll do it?

Jake: Oh, that thing that you asked me?

Moremi: Ja, ja.

Jake: Ok, no problem.

Moremi: Ok that’s good, but I hope we’ll get the old man today. This morning.

Jake: Ok no problem.

Moremi: Ja, just keep quiet, sharp?

Jake: Ok, sharp. Bye.

Sound Up Jake
This was the time he phoned me at four o clock in the morning, I was still half asleep. And that’s when he phoned me and he told me that my agreement still stands. That was that R40 000 he’s talking about.

Voice
Mr Adam was successfully rescued later that day after police were able to identify the kidnappers.

Moremi has since been charged by the Hawks, and appeared in court on two counts of corruption. At that time he declined to comment.

Sound Up Moremi
Moremi: I don’t want to fucking say anything.

Man: We’re not talking to the media sorry Graham.

Voice
And he wasn’t too happy about being asked questions.

Sound Up Moremi hits camera

Voice
But in a response sent via his attorney, he did say the following:

“I can confidently say I never demanded a R40 000 bribe from anyone.”

And, “I am happy that the allegations will be tested in court and if it’s found that I demanded a bribe, I will be the first to welcome the sanction that will be imposed on me. Equally if it’s found that the charges/allegations were fabricated, those responsible will have to answer.”

Link Derek
Even if there is a positive outcome to a kidnapping incident, the traumatised victims and their families are often left to deal with the tragedy for years to come.

Sound Up Jake
Derek: What has happened to the family now?

Jake: The family is still scared… They’re planning to leave.

Derek: And you say you’re just fearing for your life now?

Jake: I’m fearing for my life, I’m just very scared. I don’t know what else he can plan to do.

Voice
And in the absence of a police force trained, equipped and corruption free enough to adequately deal with kidnappings, it’s not a problem that’s going away anytime soon.

Sound Up Herman
Derek: We’ve heard how kidnappings in Nigeria are a business, are we seeing red lights now here in South Africa?

Herman: I honestly believe that we need to do much more in this country, to prevent it, to address it, to investigate it then what we currently do. ENDS






Promos
Promo1 (21 sec)

Voice
Imagine going through the trauma of having a loved one kidnapped, only to allegedly be asked to hand over cash for their safe return from the same police officer investigating the case.

Sound Up Jake
Derek: Jake this is a policeman, asking for a bribe…

Jake: Ja

Derek: to find an elderly man who’d been kidnapped?

Jake: Kidnapped, ja.





Promo 2 (21 sec)

Voice
In a Carte Blanche exclusive, we expose how a senior police officer allegedly wanted R40 000 in cash for the safe return of a kidnapping victim.

Sound Up Jake
And that’s when he phoned me and he told me that my agreement still stands. That was that R40 000 he’s talking about.

Voice
An insider’s look at the dark under belly of kidnappings in South Africa.




Promo 3 (11 sec)
In a country where kidnappings are on the rise, you’d hope that the police are doing their best to stop the scourge. But what do you do when an officer demands a bribe to save a victim?

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We expose corruption at the highest levels within the SAPS, as leaked audio recordings implicate the head of a kidnapping taskforce in extorting his already traumatised victims.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have access to audio recordings of the head of the Crime Intelligence Hostage Rescue team, or HICR, where he is asking for a R40 000 bribe from a family, to solve the case in which their father, a wealthy businessman, was kidnapped. No one else has what we have, and no other media are onto it yet. We would break the story.
metadata.Summary: On the 10th of March this year, Amrath Natha was kidnapped for ransom from his business premises in Johannesburg. Amrath had become the latest victim in an ever increasing crime wave that's hit South Africa's Indian communities, where businessmen are often targeted, kidnapped, and huge ransom's demanded from the distraught families for their release. In Natha's case, the kidnappers were demanding R5 million from the family. The family employed a private security company, and contacted the SAPS for help. The security company, Watchdogz, employed a private investigator named Reshaad Ismail, who was well known for dealing with kidnappings, and who had a good relationship with the head of the kidnapping task team, Col "Touch" Moreme. But as Ismail kept upping the amount he wanted for the work, Watchdogz terminated his employment. Soon thereafter, the family spokesperson, Hiren Rama was called by Col Moreme, and asked to be paid an amount to solve the case. Rama told Watchdogz security about the call, and they contacted the Hawks Anti Corruption unit. Rama started recording the phone - calls between himself and Moreme. In two seperate audio recordings, Moreme can be heard negotiating a price of R40 000. At one point he lowers it to R20 000, but later asks for R40 000 again. We also have further conversations where the money and delivery of the money is discussed.
metadata.Further information: The Hawks tried to catch Moreme receiving the money in a sting operation, but before that could be finalised Amrath Natha was found safe. The Hawks have obtained the audio recordings and witness statements about the incident, and according to our information Col Moreme has been served with a J175 summons to appear in court relating to charges for the above mentioned on the 12th November 2021. The Natha family are absolutely terrified of speaking, or even being mentioned in the insert. Amrath Natha is still undergoing trauma counseling, and they are immigrating to another country within the next few days. The family spokesperson has agreed to be interviewed if we hide his identity. The family have requested we not mention their names at all - this is a setback but also quite understandable considering the circumstances. We can tell the story using pseudonyms and recreations, as well as the audio recordings. It seems strange that the prosecutor did not issue an arrest warrant, but rather just the summons. We should ask the NPA why that is. We will have to give both Ismail and Moreme right's of reply. Watchdogz Security owner Fuad Vally willing to tell what he knows of the story.
